Description: Transcribed from volume 39 of the Kashmir Series of Texts and Studies. Notes: Date entered by the staff of Muktabodha under the supervision of Mark S. G. Dyczkowski. Revision 0: August 01, 2006.

Oṃ, salutations to Paramaśiva, whose body is pure consciousness.
Now.
The *Śrīvātūlanāthasūtrāṇi*,
together with the commentary composed by the venerable Anantaśaktipāda. [The state] in which modifications have arisen through the power of the friction and impact of union—

I bow to that supreme boldness, accessible only through the mouth of the Guru, which is the state of void beyond the void, the essence of imperishable awakening, and which shines everywhere through the gaze of the sky-farer (khecarī).

May that unborn one, whose nature is the unsurpassed sky of consciousness, be victorious— he who, through the mode of transcending all things in this world, is homeless and beyond all sequence yet possesses the power of sequence.
I bow to that which arises from the ocean of the heart of the illustrious Vātūlanātha, and which is utterly devoid of the worshiper, the object of worship, and the act of worship.
By means of which, although always situated in the midst of all fluctuations here,
I remain stainless, fully absorbed in the Great Space within this [Self].
I bow to that unsurpassed [Reality], which is without prior cause, without entry, without touch, and without abode— the grinding away of consciousness, conceptualization, and volition.
An excellent commentary on the sūtras born from the mouth of the Yoginī is being composed by someone, perfectly augmented by the supreme reality. (6)
(p. 2) Here, indeed,

[resides] the Mistress of the Seat (pīṭheśvarī) of the venerable Vātūlanātha, who transcends all philosophical systems— from the six schools and the four traditions up to the melāpa— and who is ineffable.
Having spoken the Ucchuṣmapādauha, thereafter,
with a vision that directly realizes the thirteen discourses augmented by the supreme secret,

[he describes that which is] free from the stains of succession and non-succession, existence and non-existence, truth and untruth, difference and non-difference, and the conceptual and non-conceptual states of worldly existence and nirvāṇa.
They point toward a certain supreme reality that allows no other possibility through the medium of aphorisms—wherein this first aphorism states:
"The attainment of one's own true nature occurs through the Great Sāhasa commentary. (1)
For someone who has been struck by an exceedingly intense, even more intense, and unimpeded descent of power (*śaktipāta*),
and who is thus absorbed in their own true nature, there may arise at some time and in some place, quite spontaneously,
through the "mode of great audacity" (*mahāsāhasavṛtti*), an expansion consisting of the vibrant resonance of another Name that is voracious and most profound.

Through the friction of the entire mass of cognitions consisting of both conceptual and non-conceptual forms, by means of the steadfast immersion in unobstructed great emptiness (*nirāvaraṇa-mahāśūnyatā*), there is the "attainment of one's true nature" (*svarūpalābha*) due to having transcended all mental constructions.

The secret meaning is this: there occurs the attainment of a consciousness that is uncreated, without occasion, unsurpassable, waveless, limitless, homeless, and untouchable. Furthermore, the entry into the practice of great daring (mahāsāhasavṛtti) is to be understood through the sequence that will be explained hereafter. || 1 ||

(p. 3) Having described the oral tradition (*carcā-sampradāya*) of the great courage that consists in the direct realization of the nature of the homeless state through the method of instantaneous transcendence of all [levels], [the author] now, in that very same context...

They declare that the great state of equilibrium (*sāmarasya*) of all functional modes (*vṛtti*) occurs at one and the same time; through the attainment of that, there is a simultaneous engagement of the various modes.
Likewise for the modes in the form of the rays of sight and the other senses.

"Simultaneously," meaning at the same time, by "transgressing the sequence" through a non-sequential operation of those [powers] characterized by the manifestation of passion, aversion, and so forth; "suffused by that attainment," meaning by the attainment of one's own essential nature (svarūpa) which is reached through the process of immersion into the previously mentioned state of great audacity (mahāsāhasa).

"Non-functioning" (*apravṛtti*)— meaning a state of constant abiding through immersion in That, by virtue of being never-falling away— is "thoroughly pervaded," that is, touched and brought to its own true nature, by the Great Effortless One (*mahānirīha*), whose body is the all-sufficient devouring (*alaṃgrāsa*) that transcends the conceptualization of time and non-time. This is the meaning conveyed by this particular mode of expression.

The meaning is that immediately after all mental fluctuations (*vṛtti*), there is a constant abiding within the very expanse of arising— in the form of the abode (*dhāma*) which is the great void transcending all— by becoming one with it through the dissolution of mutual distinctions. || 2 ||

P. 4) Having thus explained the instruction on simultaneous narration through this method of expression, they now describe the discourse on the book: "From the unfolding of both flaps, one enters the great emptiness."

At the time of the grace bestowed by the venerable Niṣkriyānandanātha, that attainment in the supreme state which was taught by the venerable Siddha of Gandhamādana through the presentation of an uncreated book is now being explained in detail.
The arising of the flow of the vital breath (prāṇa), which consists of the manifestation of the seven-flamed [fire] emerging through the sequence of the seven apertures,
is itself the upper tablet (ūrdhvapaṭṭaka), the arising of the full activity.
The lower tablet (adhaḥpaṭṭaka) is of the nature of the downward breath (apāna), extending through the flow of the channel of the two apertures and the void.
Enveloped by the power of the five senses, situated below, and bound by the nature of the five hoods;
having unsealed his two coils consisting of waking and dreaming and having removed the binding of the knots—
by "the lifting of both bands," that is, by the piercing of the pair of prāṇa and apāna— he who resides in the center...
Having the nature of the vital breath (*prāṇa*), its essence is great emptiness; it is free from the state of conceptualizing the "families" and "non-families," inexpressible, the great unobstructed,
devoid of both the object of knowledge and the knower, and transcending color, non-color, and the absence of color.

Devoid of the manifestation of contact and non-contact, it is designated by such terms as "the Supreme Space" (paramākāśa) and so forth through metaphorical usage. In this context, "entry" refers to the state of aesthetic equilibrium (sāmarasya) resulting from immersion into that [reality]. That indeed is it.
The meaning is that [the state] named "having attained the great instruction" manifests. || 3 ||
Thus, according to the perspective taught in the Mahānaya, because it transcends the proliferation of all treatises, there is something ineffable—
the direct realization of the Great Instruction— by means of the cessation of the duality of existence and non-existence in the form of the two tablets.

Having made known the immersion into the great void, which is free from all immersions and consists of the entry into the waveless supreme sky, the fruit of liberation is now described through identification with that [void] by means of the concluding summary of the couple.
Through the swallowing of the pairs, consciousness comes to rest in the state of non-distinction.

Within each of the five great elements, beginning with earth, there is an established arrangement of a dual functioning arising through the relationship of the grasped and the grasper. In that regard, because of the predominance of smell, the earth-principle (dharātattva) possesses a twofold nature in the form of the anus and the nose; and likewise for the water-principle (aptattva).

Due to the predominance of taste (*rasa*), there is a twofold manifestation in the form of the genitals and the tongue. Because the fire element (*tejas-tattva*) has form (*rūpa*) as its primary quality, it exists in two forms through the distinction between the feet and the eyes. Because the air element (*vāyu-tattva*) has touch (*sparśa*) as its primary quality, it proceeds in two ways by way of the nature of the skin and the hands. [The same applies to] the space element (*ākāśa-tattva*).
Due to the predominance of sound, its multiplicity arises from the very duality of speech and hearing.

Alternatively, those whose nature is earth and water abide as the objects of enjoyment (*bhogya*), while those called fire and air abide as the subjects of enjoyment (*bhoktṛ*). And this ether (*ākāśa*) stands between this pair, by virtue of its being perfectly porous.
It has arisen within all the channels (p.

6) and is divided in many ways; [it consists of] the four elements from earth to air as the object of enjoyment, and space as the nature of the enjoyer—or rather, even within the object of enjoyment, the enjoyer is always present.

It abides; even in the enjoyer, enjoyment eternally shines forth. The intended meaning is that, according to the reasoning thus stated, each of the five great elements, beginning with earth, incessantly flashes forth through a pair—that is, by means of a twofold manifestation. Alternatively, [they shine] individually as manifest and unmanifest, or as external and internal.

Or it shines forth through the state of being either quiescent or predominant. Through the "devouring"—that is, the withdrawal—of the pair situated in these five locations, there arises the "abiding in consciousness that admits no interval" (*niravakāśasaṃvinniṣṭhā*). This refers to the firm establishment of that consciousness which admits no interval, by virtue of its being perfectly non-erroneous. Nor is it [defined] merely by the quality of being consciousness that admits no interval...

No opportunity is gained through the unfoldings of conceptual consciousness (*savikalpa-saṃvit*), nor is entry attained by means of the nature of non-conceptual consciousness (*nirvikalpa-saṃvit*). Thus, because it is immeasurable and because its nature is the unsurpassed supreme non-duality (*niruttara-paramādvaya*), this consciousness is here called "without opportunity" (*niravakāśa*). This is its culmination.
The meaning is that for some, there arises a constant state of non-falling away (acyuta-gati) through the vision shown by the supreme Guru.

Thus, by means of the swallowing (kavalana) of the Kula and Kaula which consist of these two aspects, there arises identity with that which is free from limiting conditions (nirupādhinī), formless (nirūpa), and devoid of specific nature (niḥsvarūpa). || 4 ||

(p. 7) Having here explained the abiding in the supreme reality (*paratattva*) through the dissolution of duality by means of the progression of the discourse on the couple (*yugmacarcā*), thereupon the direct realization of the discourse on union (*saṃghaṭṭa*) is described: "From the union of the Siddhas and Yoginīs arises the Great Conjunction (*mahāmelāpa*). (5)
The *siddhayoginīs* are those who are both perfected ones (*siddhas*) and yoginīs; they are the embodiments of the sovereign goddesses of the sense objects and the faculties.

Their *saṃghaṭṭa*—their union, the mutual embrace consisting of the conjunction of both the grasped and the grasper—is an embrace through the process of mutual incitement. By means of that embrace, always...
The phrase "the arising of the great confluence" (*mahāmelāpodayaḥ*) means that through the dissolution of the duality consisting of "I-ness" and "this-ness," there occurs a constant arising—

that is, a full manifestation— of the nature of the great state of aesthetic equilibrium (*mahāsāmarasya*), which is directly perceptible everywhere within the unsurpassed sky of consciousness (*niruttaracidvyoman*). This occurs by way of the non-manifestation of the duality of the object of knowledge and the subject who knows.
It is thus stated that the supreme immersion into non-duality is present everywhere. || 5 ||

Having described the perpetual emergence of the Great Union (*mahāmelāpa*) through the simultaneous dissolution of both [subject and object], they then indicate the attainment of the unsurpassed state by transcending the three coverings (*kañcuka*):
"By abandoning the three coverings, there is abiding in the ineffable state (*nirākhyapada*). (6)
Of the three-fold sheath (*trikañcuka*), which is divided into the categories of the real (*bhāvika*), the elemental (*bhautika*), and the void (*śūnya*): (p.
8) therein, the "real" consists of that which begins with sound and ends with the ego-principle (*ahaṃkāra*), having the nature of the subtle elements (*tanmātra*);
the "elemental" has the form of earth and so forth; and the "void" is that which is called "inactive" (*nirīha*) and has the nature of latent impressions (*vāsanā*).

Alternatively, the "existent" (bhāvika) is the external form of the jar, which is the nature of the object to be grasped; the "elemental" (bhautika), moreover, is the internal nature of the sense organ, which is the nature of the act of grasping; and the "void" (śūnya) is the space between those two. Alternatively, the "existent" is said to be the creation of the dream state.
The manifestation of the material world is called the waking state (*jāgrat*), and the void is designated as the state of deep sleep (*suṣupta*);

this is described as the withdrawal (*saṃhāra*). By the "renunciation" or abandonment of the threefold sheath (*trikañcuka*) established in this manner, there occurs "abiding in the ineffable state" (*nirākhyapadāvasthiti*), that which has transcended all names and designations.

The connection [of the verse] is as follows: "Nameless" means indefinable, unsurpassed, transcending speech, the supreme abode; in that supreme space which is the dwelling-place transcending all, there is a state of constant abiding, a firm establishment in one's own nature from which there is never any falling away. || 6 ||
Having thus described the attainment of the fourth state through the transcendence of the three sheaths,
they now demonstrate that within all manifestations of speech, which are entirely unobstructed, there always shines forth only the unfolding of the phonemes and their elemental powers.
The vowel manifests within the expansions of the arising and the cessation of the fourfold speech.
First, the fourfold speech is determined:

its nature is the expansion of the first vibration (*spanda*), which consists of a slight movement surging forth within the supreme sky that is unobscured, without interval, arising, unsurpassed, and waveless.

It is renowned as *parā* because it internalizes the arrangement of phonemes (*varṇaracanā*) through the non-dual great state of aesthetic integration (*advayamahāsāmarasya*), according to the analogy of the fluid within a peacock's egg. And that very [power], having attained the nature of the unstruck sound (*anāhatanāda*),
possesses an indivisible character and internalizes the emergence of all phonemes, like the seed-pod of a banyan tree.

She is designated as *paśyantī* because she perceives with the nature of the seer. And that very same [power], having assumed the ground of the intellect consisting of the certainty of the multitude of conceptual constructions and mental fluctuations, and internalizing the mass of phonemes according to the analogy of the seed-pod (*śimbikāphala*), is called *madhyamā*. That same [power]...
Striking [the air] through the sequence of places and articulators such as the heart, throat, and palate,
she manifests differentiated forms— like verses composed of the wealth of phonemes— and brings about the manifestation of the entire cosmic display of form and so forth; thus she is called Vaikharī.
In this way, from the state of consciousness (*saṃvit*) which admits no interval, the fourfold speech unfolds incessantly and without obstruction.

Thus, for this fourfold speech of such a nature, its emergence and its cessation—those two, emergence and cessation—are respectively emission (*sṛṣṭi*) and withdrawal (*saṃhāra*); the manifestation of these two always surges forth incessantly, both manifest and unmanifest.
Vibrating— within them (p.
10)— the ‘sound’ (*svara*), whose nature is the expansion and blossoming of the Great Sound (*mahānāda*) transcending the unstruck (*anāhata*) and struck (*hata*),
‘manifests’ as the very emergence of the supreme ether (*paraviyat*) which transcends both conceptual and non-conceptual consciousness.
The meaning is that [the subject] proceeds by way of constant engagement in non-action (*akaraṇa*).
Thus, from among the risings of the multitude of phonemes— which consist of the manifestation of the unfolding of various distinctions—
one proceeds through each successive phoneme by means of the sequence of the fourfold speech (*vākcatuṣṭaya*), with an uninterrupted function, without abandoning one’s own essential nature.
It is thus stated that, according to the principle taught by the very face [of the teacher], the sound itself resounds. || 7 ||

Having thus determined that the unobscured rising of the vowels (svarodaya) vibrates everywhere and at all times through the sequence of the emergence of the fourfold speech, it is now stated that when there is the enjoyment of the triad of rasas, the supreme abode alone shines forth as unsurpassed.
Through the tasting of the three flavors, the Supreme Brahman—free from bonds and surging forth without desire—is realized. || 8 ||

The three flavors (rasatraya) are briefly revealed through the perspective taught from the mouth of the Guru. When there is the full enjoyment of the threefold natural flavor (akṛtrima-rasatritaya), renowned as being established in the Mūlādhāra and the Payodharādhāra, that which has "surged forth without desire" (anicchocchalita)—
meaning it has blossomed free from longing— and is "devoid of bonds" (vigatabandha), meaning it is free from the manifestation of duality that constitutes saṃsāra— [is realized].

The meaning is that the Supreme Brahman itself— transcending both the peaceful and the variegated forms of Brahman, and possessing a nature of consciousness consisting of an ineffable and most excellent reflective awareness— continually unfolds through an unceasing state. This very point is stated according to the secret tradition.

The *mūlādhāra* (root-support), however, is the first manifestation of creative splendor (*pratibhollāsa*), characterized by the Great Sound (*mahānāda*), and is of the nature of emanation (*sṛṣṭi*); for it serves as the foundational wall for the primary locus of the categories of consciousness, which consist of both difference and non-difference. The *payodhara* (cloud/supporter), moreover, because it nourishes all through its "water" (*payaḥ*), maintains that very same nature of consciousness which is the support of all.

The vibration (*spanda*) which supports stability and growth is indeed the primordial unfolding (*ādyonmeṣa*), for it takes the form of stability because it illuminates all objects. The support, however, is withdrawal (*saṃhāra*), whose nature is the consciousness of reversion, because it withdraws the categories of insentient and sentient entities. That which arises from these three is the nature of aesthetic flavor (*rasa*), and following that—

The secret meaning is this: having savored the state of aesthetic identity (*sāmarasya*) with the wonder of phenomenal existence and having contemplated it through entry into the uncreated seal of emptiness within one's own self, the nature of the Fourth State (*turya*), known as the Great Withdrawal (*mahāsaṃhāra*), shines forth incessantly as supreme non-duality. || 8 ||
Having thus established the tradition of the discourse on the three *rasas* through an irrefutable method,
the direct realization of the narrative of the four goddesses is now revealed (p. 12),
[which occurs] always through the manifestation of the four goddesses.
The state of abiding in one's own repose. || 9 ||

The four goddesses are known as Hunger (*kṣud*), Thirst (*tṛṣ*), Envy (*īrṣyā*), and Thinking (*mananā*). Among them, because it is intent upon devouring everything, Hunger itself is the Great Dissolution (*mahāsaṃhāra*). Because it dries up everything, Thirst itself is the dissolution. Envy is that which brings about the manifestation of duality; it is a state bound by the grasping of subject and object. And Thinking is...

Creation consists of the manifestation of conceptualization (*saṃkalpa*) and discursive thought (*vikalpa*). Through the "expansion" (*ullāsa*)— that is, the unfolding and the flow of the devouring consciousness (*ghasmarasaṃvit*)— of this fourfold group of goddesses who possess such a nature, there occurs at all times, in each instance, an effort characterized by the appearance [of objects], their relishing, and the full grasping [of them] as the essence of one's own true nature through its fourfold selfhood.
The meaning is that the state of abiding—which transcends the fifth stage—is established as resting in consciousness that admits no other possibility. || 9 ||

Having thus revealed the sequence of the narrative of the four goddesses by means of this sūtra, the secret of the wheel of the twelve channels is now described: "Through the arising of the twelve channels, there is the blossoming of the great radiance. (10)

The five cognitive faculties, beginning with the ear, together with the mind (*manas*), as well as the five active faculties, beginning with speech, together with the intellect (*buddhi*)—the aggregate of these two is the "twelvefold flow" (*advādaśavāha*). (p.
13) Its manifestation is by some causeless, most unshackled, and unsurpassed state of being...
Through the operation of independence from other limbs, there is a flow of voracious consciousness. By that means, within each individual flow,

there occurs the "expansion" of the rays of great consciousness— consisting of exertion, manifestation, savoring, full grasping, and rest— of the great rays [of light] in a process of unobstructed succession, [encompassing] the determined and undetermined sentient and insentient.

The meaning of the great statement (mahāvākyārtha) is this: through the non-dissolution of manifestation, the Great Awakening—whose nature is eternally blossoming—abides at all times, everywhere, and in every way, by virtue of its perpetual indestructibility. || 10 ||

Having thus revealed, by means of the vision of the arising of the twelve-fold flow, that which is established as non-action—the perpetual immersion in the state free from obscuration—they now describe the tradition of the fivefold conduct:
"In the arising of the fivefold conduct, there is immersion free of waves. (11)

The *Caryāpañcaka*, however, consists of the essential nature of the Anāśrita, Avadhūta, Unmatta, Sarvabhakṣya, and Mahāvyāpaka. Its arising (*udaya*) is the expansion (*ullāsa*), whose nature is blossoming, emerging from within the collection of both fixed and unfixed powers (*śakti*). When that [arising] exists, there occurs "waveless immersion" (*nistaraṅga-samāveśa*), which is the emergence of the *āṇava*, *śākta*, and *śāmbhava* states.

The meaning is that it expands as the very nature of the unsurpassed immersion (*samāveśa*), characterized by an immersion free from all waves of form. And I shall explain in detail the sequence of the fivefold conduct (*caryā*). In that regard, [the state] is "unsupported" because it lacks a foundation; it has the nature of the supreme space (*paramākāśa*) by way of entering the region of the cavity of the ear.

She has arisen for the purpose of withdrawing her own objects of perception; she is the *avadhūtā* (the shaken-off), awakened through the power of vision on the path of wandering everywhere due to her lack of fixedness, in order to appropriate that which is to be withdrawn by herself; and she is the *unmattā* (the madwoman), who, through her independence like one devoid of mind, disregards the relationship between subject and object in order to grasp her own domain.

She is renowned as the consumer of all; she is characterized by devouring every edible and non-edible preparation, having arisen for the purpose of swallowing whatever objects can be withdrawn by her own power. And she is all-pervasive, having manifested for the sake of appropriating every touch, because she extends through the entire range of the skin. Thus.
The Arising of the Fivefold Conduct. || 11 ||
Having examined the sequence of the practice of perpetual accomplishment,
they now examine the discourse on the cessation of merit and demerit by relying upon the illumination of supreme gnosis that is free from abode.
Through immersion in Great Awakening (mahābodha), there is no connection with merit or sin;
and "Great Awakening" is that which is free from the turbidity of the conceptual constructions and volitions of knower, knowledge, and the knowable—(p.
15)—consisting of the expansion of the light that is the abode of the cessation of all agitation and the ultimate tranquility, the nature of supreme knowledge itself.
The Great Teachers have directly realized Being (bhāva) because it transcends both succession and non-succession.

Its "immersion" (samāveśa) consists in its constant manifestation as that very form—by way of abandoning, accepting, and relinquishing through the process of non-action, and by remaining in its natural state without ever falling away from its own function. Therefore:

"Through immersion in Great Awakening (mahābodhasamāveśāt)," there occurs for a certain Vīravara— who is of his final birth and lives perpetually— the "non-connection," that is, the non-adhesion and non-union, with both merit and demerit, i.e., with the two types of karma characterized as auspicious and inauspicious, which by nature bestow their respective fruits, [this state] being at all times uncreated.

The meaning is that for one who is fully satiated by the relishing of the flavor of experience, the great liberation—which transcends both bondage and liberation—stands within this very world of existence like an amalaka fruit in the palm of one's hand. || 12 ||
Having explained the sequence of discourse concerning the setting aside of merit and demerit preceded by the attainment of one's own true nature,
they now introduce the discourse on naturally established silence through the power of the "discourse of non-discourse," which is the seal of great wonder.
Through attainment, there is the state of the natural sound. || 13 ||

The power of the discourse on the "Inexpressible" (akathanakathā) is here briefly discussed according to the sequence of the oral tradition (*saṃpradāya*) taught by the mouth of the Guru. (p. 16) The exposition of this letter *a*, which has arisen in four forms by way of being struck (*hata*), unstruck (*anāhata*), struck-unstruck (*anāhata-hata*), and transcending the unstruck (*anāhata-hatot-tīrṇa*), consists of the arrangement of the discussion of the oral lineage (*vaktrāmnāya*).

This is the explanation of the "struck" (hata) and the "unstruck" (anāhata). Among these, the "struck" is first described: it is that which, through the arrangement of the places of articulation (sthāna) and the organs of production (karaṇa), such as the heart, throat, palate, and so forth, manifests various objects beginning with the letter *a* and ending with the letter *ha*. The "unstruck," on the other hand, is the expansion of the supreme sound (*paranāda*) arising from the root of the toneless (*asvara*), which serves as the symbolic convention for the middle note (*madhyamā-svara*) of the lute strings.

Having established its presence through metaphorical usage from the navel down to the edge of the ear-cavity, it is both struck and unstruck. Arising from the space situated between the two ears—which is supported by both [the physical and the metaphysical]—it is "unstruck" (anāhata) when resting, yet "struck" (hata) when manifested through the resonance of the auditory passage, the protection of the ear-canal, and the emergence of its expansion. It is "unstruck" even in its reflection upon reality, arising from the body of reality itself.

*Hatahata*. Transcending even the *anāhatahata*, it is the resonance (*svara*) that shines forth in the abode of the Great Unobscured (*mahānirāvaraṇadhāma*), which is free from conceptual construction (*avikalpa*).

It is the primordial limit (*prathamakoṭi*) of the Great Vibration (*mahāspanda*) characterized by slight movement; because it is devoid of contraction and expansion, it is the form of supreme expansion. Being beyond the nature of touch, it consists of the manifestation of the Great Mantra (*mahāmantra*) that cannot be uttered.
And thus, that which has transcended both the unstruck (*anāhata*) and the struck (*hata*) is the fourth state (*turya*), shaped like a *śṛṅgāṭaka* (water-chestnut) and having the nature of Raudrī.
That which is both unstruck and struck has the form of a face consisting of the vowel-less energy (*anackakalā*) and is of the nature of Vāmā; it is the state of deep sleep (*suṣupta*).
And the unstruck is the power Ambikā, who is of the form of the arm, as stated in the Āgama.

(p. 17) Dream is described as having that [dreaming] nature; and waking is the nature of the eldest [state], characterized by the form of weapons. This description of the first letter, which possesses the nature of this tetrad, is a specific method of reasoning through the gateway of tradition. Its power is the resonance (*rāva*) that transcends the "struck" (*hata*), arising from the three forms beginning with the "struck."

Vīrya is the nature of throbbing radiance; by means of that "power of the ineffable discourse," it is as follows: therein, the ineffable is speech transcending the proliferation of conceptual elaboration (*prapañca*). This very ineffability is the discourse itself, which, through the process of transition, is the realization of the nature of the homeless state.
That alone is the power, the essence of unconditioned expansion. By means of that, there is transition.

A little is here elaborated: when the excellent teacher, having established his seat in the abode of consciousness— which is blossoming without waves— through the dissolution of the conceit residing in the limited subjects consisting of the vital breath (*prāṇa*),

the subtle body (*puryaṣṭaka*), and the void (*śūnya*), [acts] by the power of the vision of the supreme void, beautiful with motionless bliss, and being independent of effects, instruments, and actions, whatever [he may do]...
Upon the realization of the nature of the omnipresent Self, one perceives that everything is constantly nothing but the supreme consciousness itself;
of this there is no doubt. Accordingly, he states another interpretation:

"The teaching [is found] within the collections of the six systems of philosophy (*ṣaddarśana*), the four traditions (*caturāmnāya*), and the sequence of the *melāpa*, concerning the rules established in the sequence of worship."
Those [rays] flash forth by means of relying upon the wheel of the specific deity.

Here, however, by abandoning the relationship between the worshipper, the worshipped, and the act of worship, there is simply the constant expansion of the great rays, according to the oral tradition of the preeminent Siddhas such as the venerable Vātūlanātha.

The connection is as follows: because he shines everywhere at all times, inseparable from the nature that transcends everything, the power of this "discourse on the non-discourse" brings about the attainment of great wonder (*mahāvismaya*). And "great wonder" means that *smaya*—the pride of limited or unlimited egoism—is gone, destroyed, through the function of transcending all things.

It is the penetration into one's own essential nature (*svarūpa*). And yet, it is a great wonder: because of the forgetting of the distinction between self and other, there is an instantaneous immersion into the activity of the sky-farer (*khecarī*) that is uninterrupted and unimpeded. That very state is called "seal" (*mudrā*) because it embraces all seals; its essence consists in immersion into the state of silence (*mauna-pada*). By means of that [state] acting as the cause—

The term *khasvaratā* means that there occurs the manifestation of *sāmarasya* (homogeneous equilibrium), which is the state (*bhāva*) of *khasvara*. *Khasvara* is so called because it pervades (*rāti*), encompasses (*vyāpnoti*), and assimilates (*svīkaroti*) even the void (*kha*), which is itself devoid of objective existence (*bhāva-śūnya*). Thus, it is *khasvara*. || 13 ||

By way of instruction on the direct realization of the thirteen discourses— the discourse of the universal assembly of all those belonging to the four traditions of the six philosophical systems— through the non-duality of the unsurpassed state, at the time of the Great Assembly (mahāmelāpa) in the presence of certain Avadhūtas and the Mistress of the Sacred Seats (pīṭheśvarīs).

The method of the speaker, as established in the Sūtra, has been revealed. For the sake of the understanding of the wise, this commentary (*vṛtti*) on that very [work] has been composed by us here in brief. May there be auspiciousness! Thus ends the supreme secret, which is free from the flood of conceptual constructions of speech.
By someone who is perfectly liberated from the delusion of the distinction between existence and non-existence,
through the expansion of consciousness and by means of an activity characterized by the unimpeded, intense joy of supreme being, this incomparable and sublime work has been composed.
This commentary on the *Śrīmadvātūlanāthasūtra* is complete.
It is the work of the venerable Anantaśaktipāda,
composed for the pleasure of the virtuous by the command of the illustrious King Pratāpa.
